project.name: myclash
project.description: Free, open-source platform for HEMA (Historical European Martial Arts) tournament management and result publication. An offline-first, per-event-themed monorepo spanning NestJS API, three Next.js PWAs, a static marketing site, and shared workspace packages. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: What MyClash Is
tour.description: Start with the project README to understand MyClash's purpose: a free, open-source platform for running HEMA (Historical European Martial Arts) tournaments end-to-end and publishing results. It lays out the three founding convictions (offline-first scoring, per-exchange data as source of truth, per-event theming), the four-app + shared-package monorepo layout, and the 14-service production stack. AGENTS.md complements it with the hard rules every contributor must respect, most importantly: never bypass the ruleset engine, and raw exchanges are the only source of truth.

tour.title: The Architecture Map
tour.description: Before reading code, study the canonical architecture specification. It describes the product surfaces (public, scoring, admin, marketing), the tech stack, the system architecture, the data model, and the TF_v1 ruleset plugin system that the rest of the tour will revisit in code. Treat this as the authoritative reference whenever a later step feels disconnected from the whole.

tour.title: API Bootstrap & Wiring
tour.description: The NestJS API is the heart of the backend, and main.ts is its runtime entry point: it creates the app, wires global exception filters and request-logging middleware, applies HTTP security, and starts the server on port 4000. app.module.ts is the composition root with the highest fan-out in the codebase (41) — it imports every feature module (events, phases, matches, referees, auth, admin, and more) and registers the global guards and interceptors. Reading these two files gives you a bird's-eye view of every domain the platform handles.
tour.languageLesson: NestJS uses a module system built on dependency injection: @Module decorators declare providers (services) and controllers, and the framework wires them together at startup. The root AppModule importing every feature module is the standard NestJS composition-root pattern.

tour.title: The Data Model
tour.description: The foundational migration 0001_init.sql creates the 33 core tables — organizations, clubs, fighters, events, tournaments, phases, pools, matches, exchanges, referees, and workshops — that model the entire domain. The Drizzle events schema then mirrors this in TypeScript: an event is the gathering (e.g. Swordfish 2027), carrying per-event theming and lices (the fighting arenas/pistes). This is the vocabulary every later step depends on, so it is worth understanding the event → tournament → phase → pool → match → exchange hierarchy here.
tour.languageLesson: SQL migrations are applied in numbered order and should be idempotent and reversible — the schema evolves incrementally from 0001 onward. Drizzle then defines the same tables as typed TypeScript objects, giving compile-time safety over the raw SQL model.

tour.title: Security & Realtime Foundations
tour.description: Two cross-cutting concerns underpin every feature. The RLS migration establishes Postgres row-level security policies granting role-based access to platform admins, organizers, staff, and public visitors — the data layer enforces authorization, not just the API. The realtime migration configures Supabase publications so matches, exchanges, and notifications stream live to clients, which is what makes the spectator and scoring apps feel instant. supabase.service.ts (the single most depended-upon file, fan-in 118) is the thin wrapper every module uses to reach the database and auth.

tour.title: Events & Tournaments
tour.description: Building on the data model from Step 4, the events module is the primary domain entry point. events.service.ts orchestrates Supabase access for event and tournament CRUD, publishing, dashboard stats, public standings, pool/bracket views, and media uploads, while the controller exposes those operations as REST endpoints. This is where an organizer's event first comes to life before it gets a schedule, pools, or matches.

tour.title: Schedule & Programme
tour.description: Once an event exists, it needs a timetable. The schedule-grid service orders matches and programme blocks across pistes and produces a renderable timetable using canonical round codes, while the programme controller manages the non-match blocks (ceremonies, breaks, workshops) that share the same arenas. Together they turn the abstract event into a concrete day-of-event plan that both organizers and spectators rely on.

tour.title: Pools & Brackets
tour.description: Tournaments run in phases: pool play followed by elimination brackets. phases.service.ts is the central phase engine that generates pools and brackets and manages membership, rescheduling, and visibility. pool-generator.ts produces balanced pools via snake seeding and local-search optimization (delegating to the shared scheduling package), and bracket-advance.service.ts progresses winners and losers through slots as matches complete, resolving byes and lazily creating downstream matches. This is the competition's structural backbone.

tour.title: The Ruleset Engine
tour.description: MyClash's defining principle is that scores are always derived, never stored — and the @myclash/rulesets package is where that derivation lives. types.ts defines the pure, side-effect-free Ruleset contract plus the domain types (Match, Exchange, Pool, Standings) every ruleset implements, and tf_v1 is the canonical implementation defining standings columns and the tiebreaker chain. The package barrel re-exports the registry, match-format/forfeit/penalty config, and scoring formulas. Per AGENTS.md, no other code may compute scores directly — everything routes through here.
tour.languageLesson: The Ruleset interface is a plugin contract: a pure, side-effect-free abstraction that lets multiple scoring systems (TF_v1, Generic_PointsCap, custom formulas) be swapped without touching the modules that consume them. Pure functions make scoring deterministic and trivially testable.

tour.title: Matches & Scoring Derivation
tour.description: This step connects the ruleset engine from Step 9 to live data. matches.service.ts orchestrates match CRUD, exchange recording and editing, scheduling, locking, referee resolution, and bracket population after a match completes. scoring.service.ts is deliberately thin: it derives match scores from the recorded exchanges via the rulesets engine, reinforcing that aggregate scores are computed on demand while raw exchanges persist as the source of truth.

tour.title: The Scoring PWA
tour.description: The web-scoring app is the tablet-first, offline-first scorekeeper surface that referees use at the piste. The match page loads the raw match row and renders MatchView, the central scoreboard orchestrator that composes the header, two scoring columns, centre controls, the forfeit panel, and the corrections drawer — and owns the exchange-by-exchange submission that feeds Step 10's scoring derivation. Every tap here writes an exchange, never a score, honoring the per-exchange-truth principle from Step 1.

tour.title: The Public Spectator App
tour.description: The web-public app is the mobile-first PWA for spectators and competitors. The event layout fetches and applies per-event theming so each event feels local rather than like a generic platform, the live page shows all running and upcoming matches as realtime cards, and the live match viewer renders the scoreboard, exchange feed, and penalty feed — subscribing to Supabase realtime so the exchanges entered in Step 11 appear here within moments. This closes the loop from referee input to public results.

tour.title: The Admin Console & Shared Packages
tour.description: The web-admin app is the desktop-first organizer and super-admin surface. The schedule grid orchestrator is its most powerful screen — fetching matches and programme blocks, wiring realtime updates, drag/resize/auto-place, conflict detection, CSV export, and same-origin scoring launch — tying together everything from Steps 7, 8, and 11. All three frontends lean on shared workspaces: @myclash/ui re-exports every shared component, and @myclash/i18n holds the full EN+FR message trees plus the runtime translator that resolves dotted keys.
tour.languageLesson: A monorepo barrel (index.ts re-exporting a package's public surface) gives consumers one stable import path while letting the package reorganize internals freely. The i18n catalog enforces that every t() key exists in both EN and FR, caught by a CI lint check.

tour.title: Infrastructure, Containers & CI/CD
tour.description: Finally, see how everything ships. The API Dockerfile is a multi-stage build that installs workspace deps with pnpm, compiles the shared packages and API, then assembles a minimal non-root Alpine runtime — keeping the production image small. docker-compose.prod.yml deploys the full 14-service stack (Traefik TLS, Postgres, Redis, the Supabase suite, the API, a BullMQ worker, an ops-runner, and all four web apps) on a single VPS. The CI pipeline guards every push: build, typecheck, lint, tests, e2e, audits, and Trivy image scans.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds separate build-time deps (compilers, dev packages) from the runtime image, often cutting size by 50-80%. Layer ordering matters for cache efficiency: copy and install dependencies before app source so dependency layers are reused across builds.
